marks.description: Famille-rose Canton enamels covering the whole surface. A central roundel (often a bird or peony) is surrounded by four panels, six on large platters, that alternate figure scenes with birds, flowers and butterflies. The ground between panels is a gilt-touched scroll or diaper, often in green and pink.
marks.what_it_is: The best-known 19th-century Canton standard pattern, made almost entirely for export, mainly to North America. In Britain the same style is usually just called 'Canton'.

periods.label: Early, finest
periods.note: Howard: at its best from the 1820s until after 1860.

periods.label: Later production
periods.note: Coarser painting; 'CHINA' and 'MADE IN CHINA' marks from 1891.

periods.label: Modern
periods.note: Still made.

marks.dating_value: The pattern alone dates a piece only to c.1820 or later. Fine, crowded miniature painting, rich gilding and early Western shapes suggest before c.1860. Thin, sketchy painting and an overglaze red 'CHINA' or 'MADE IN CHINA' stamp mean 1891 or later; a 'MADE IN CHINA' mark usually means the 20th century.
marks.later_copies: Made continuously into the 20th century and still made today; late pieces are commonly marked CHINA or MADE IN CHINA in overglaze red.
marks.overlap: Shares the layout with Rose Mandarin (figures only) and Rose Canton (flowers and birds, no figures). The four-panel scheme is close to Fitzhugh.

There is no gilding. The blue ranges from grey-blue to rich cobalt and the painting is quick.
marks.what_it_is: The cheap, mass-produced blue-and-white dinner and tea ware shipped from Canton, mainly to America, from the late 18th century.

marks.later_copies: Produced from the early 19th century to the present; also imitated in English transferware as 'willow'.
marks.overlap: Nanking uses the same central landscape with a finer lattice-and-spearhead border and often gilding. Canton and Nanking were used interchangeably in some period documents.

marks.description: A Cantonese junk that left Amoy in December 1821 and sank on the Belvedere Reef. Its huge cargo of provincial Fujian and Jingdezhen blue and white (bowls, dishes, spoons) was auctioned in Stuttgart in 2000.
marks.what_it_is: A fixed point for early-Daoguang export porcelain for Southeast Asia.

periods.label: Sinking
periods.note: Left Amoy December 1821; wrecked early 1822.

marks.dating_value: Provincial blue-and-white bowls and dishes matching Tek Sing pieces can be dated c.1820.

facts.claim: The Tek Sing left Amoy in December 1821, sank on the Belvedere Reef, was rediscovered on 12 May 1999 and auctioned in Stuttgart a year later.

sources.name: Jan-Erik Nilsson, Gotheborg.com glossary: Shipwreck Tek Sing
sources.says: In December 1821 the Cantonese junk Tek Sing departed from the coastal town of Amoy... rediscovered the 12th of May 1999... put to auction in Stuttgart a year later.

conflicts: Gotheborg's page title says 'Shipwreck 1821', while the sinking itself happened in early 1822 according to most accounts (not independently verified here).

marks.description: A British country ship wrecked in the Malacca Strait on 4 March 1817, salvaged by Malaysian Historical Salvors in the 1990s; its cargo included Chinese export porcelain of the late Jiaqing period.
marks.what_it_is: A fixed point for late Jiaqing export porcelain.

periods.label: Sinking
periods.note: 4 March 1817.

marks.dating_value: Canton-type blue and white matching the Diana pieces dates to c.1817.

facts.claim: The Diana sailed on 4 March 1817 and struck the Karang Lintang reef in the Malacca Strait.

sources.name: Jan-Erik Nilsson, Gotheborg.com glossary: Shipwreck Diana
sources.says: On the 4th of March 1817, the Diana set sail up the Malacca Strait... below the water is Karang Lintang.
